title: THE MOMENT YOU QUESTION YOUR PASTOR, ARE YOU REBELLING AGAINST GOD? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH SOME CHURCHES ARE AFRAID TO CONFRONT
paragraphs: THE MOMENT YOU QUESTION YOUR PASTOR, ARE YOU REBELLING AGAINST GOD? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH SOME CHURCHES ARE AFRAID TO CONFRONT

What if the question you have been terrified to ask is not evidence of rebellion, but evidence that your conscience is still listening to God? A Scripture-anchored confrontation with spiritual authority, wounded believers, blind obedience, and the freedom Jesus never intended His Church to lose.
There is a kind of silence that sounds like holiness.
It sits quietly in church pews.
It smiles when something feels wrong.
It says “Amen” when the heart is troubled.
It raises its hands during worship while carrying questions it has been warned never to ask.
And sometimes, behind that silence, there is a Christian who is slowly falling apart.
Not because they have stopped loving Jesus.
But because they have been taught that questioning the person preaching about Jesus might mean questioning Jesus Himself.
Imagine a young woman sitting in the back of a church she once called home.
She has served faithfully for years. She has given offerings when money was tight. She has volunteered when she was exhausted. She has defended her pastor when others criticized him.
She genuinely loves her church.
But something happened.
Perhaps a teaching did not agree with Scripture.
Perhaps someone was publicly humiliated.
Perhaps financial questions were dismissed.
Perhaps a leader's behavior contradicted what he preached.
Or perhaps she simply opened her Bible one evening and discovered that a passage she had heard explained for years did not seem to mean what she had been told.
So she gathered her courage.
She asked a question.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to divide the congregation.
Not to destroy the ministry.
She just wanted to understand.
And the response shattered something inside her.
“Be careful. You're touching God's anointed.”
“Don't question spiritual authority.”
“You have a rebellious spirit.”
“Remember what happened to those who came against Moses.”
Suddenly, the issue was no longer whether her question had a biblical answer.
The issue was whether she was spiritually dangerous for asking it.
And now she sits in her car after Sunday service, gripping the steering wheel, fighting tears.
Because she cannot understand how wanting to obey God's Word somehow became an accusation of disobeying God.
Maybe you know that feeling.
Maybe you have been that person.
Or perhaps you are a pastor who has been deeply wounded by people who questioned you without kindness, spread accusations, and disguised personal ambition as spiritual discernment.
Both wounds are real.
And both deserve to be brought beneath the authority of Scripture.
Because there is a truth we desperately need to recover.
A pastor is called to shepherd God's people, not replace God's voice in their lives.
And a Christian is called to honor spiritual leadership, not surrender their conscience to another human being.
Those are not contradictory commands.
They are biblical responsibilities that belong together.
But to understand why, we need to go somewhere uncomfortable.
We need to open the Bible and allow it to confront not only abusive leadership, but also the pride, suspicion, and rebelliousness that can exist in our own hearts.
Because the Gospel does not exist to make pastors untouchable.
And it does not exist to make congregations unteachable.
It exists to bring all of us under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And that changes everything.
Consider what happened in Acts 17.
The apostle Paul was preaching the Gospel in Berea.
This was not an inexperienced teacher struggling to understand Christian doctrine.
This was Paul.
A man personally called by the risen Christ.
A man whose apostolic writings would become part of the New Testament.
If anyone could have demanded that people accept his teaching without examination, human reasoning might suggest it was him.
But Scripture tells a very different story.
Acts 17:11 says in the King James Version:
“These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.”
Read that again.
They searched the Scriptures to determine whether Paul's message was true.
And the Bible calls them noble.
Not rebellious.
Not divisive.
Not dishonoring.
Noble.
The Greek text describes them as εὐγενέστεροι (eugenesteroi), meaning more noble-minded or noble in character.
And the word translated “searched” is ἀνακρίνοντες (anakrinontes), from anakrinō, a verb that can describe examining, investigating, or carefully evaluating something.
These believers were not casually hunting for faults.
They were examining what they heard against the Scriptures they already possessed.
Their hearts were receptive, but their minds were not switched off.
And notice something beautiful.
They did not reject Paul's message simply because it challenged them.
They received it eagerly.
They investigated it carefully.
Then many believed.
Biblical discernment and spiritual openness were working together.
That is not rebellion.
That is maturity.
Now consider the implication.
If the Bereans were commended for examining the teaching of an apostle, why should any modern pastor expect his teaching to be exempt from biblical examination?
That question should not frighten a faithful shepherd.
It should encourage him.
Because a pastor who genuinely loves God's Word should rejoice when people become serious students of it.
He may need to correct misunderstandings.
He may need to explain difficult passages.
He may occasionally have to tell someone that their interpretation is mistaken.
But the goal is not to win a contest of authority.
The goal is to help people understand and obey Christ.
A faithful pastor does not need to be infallible to be respected.
He needs to be faithful, teachable, and accountable to the Lord who called him.
And a faithful congregation does not need to agree with every pastoral decision to demonstrate love.
It needs humility, discernment, and a willingness to pursue truth without cruelty.
But perhaps someone has already raised the objection.
“What about Hebrews 13:17?”
That verse matters.
We must not pretend it does not exist simply because it has sometimes been misused.
The King James Version says:
“Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account...”
Those are serious words.
Spiritual leadership is not an optional invention of organized religion.
God genuinely appoints shepherds to teach, guide, protect, and care for His people.
Hebrews 13:17 calls believers to cooperate with their leaders rather than making faithful pastoral work unnecessarily difficult.
The Greek verb πείθεσθε (peithesthe), translated “obey,” comes from peithō, which can carry the sense of being persuaded, trusting, or yielding to someone.
The word does not eliminate the obligation to heed legitimate leadership. But it helps us recognize that the relationship envisioned is not merely one of intimidation and unquestioning compliance.
The verse also uses ὑπείκετε (hypeikete), meaning to yield or give way.
There is a genuine call to humble cooperation.
Yet the verse itself contains something that should make every pastor tremble.
“They watch for your souls, as they that must give account.”
Account to whom?
Not merely a denomination.
Not merely a board.
Not merely the congregation.
Ultimately, to God.
A pastor's authority is a stewardship.
It is not personal ownership of the people entrusted to his care.
And stewardship always comes with accountability.
The passage does not teach that pastors are incapable of error, that their personal preferences are divine commands, or that questioning them is automatically sinful.
Those ideas have to be imported into the text.
They are not what the text says.
And when someone uses Hebrews 13:17 to demand obedience that contradicts God's Word, another passage becomes unavoidable.
Acts 5:29.
“We ought to obey God rather than men.”
Peter and the other apostles spoke those words while facing authorities who commanded them to stop proclaiming Jesus.
The immediate setting concerns obedience to God in the face of human prohibition.
It is not a license to dismiss every instruction we dislike.
But it establishes a principle no Christian authority can erase.
Human authority is never ultimate.
God is.
Not your favorite preacher.
Not your denomination.
Not your church's founder.
Not the person who baptized you.
Not the leader who helped you through your darkest season.
Jesus Christ alone is Lord.
And honoring those who serve Him must never become a substitute for obeying Him.
There is another passage often invoked whenever someone questions a pastor.
“Touch not mine anointed.”
Those words appear in Psalm 105:15, echoing the account of God's protection over the patriarchs.
In the King James Version, the verse says:
“Saying, Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.”
The Hebrew expression אַל־תִּגְּעוּ בִמְשִׁיחָי (ʾal-tiggeʿu vimshiḥai) carries the sense of “Do not touch my anointed ones.”
The verb נגע (nagaʿ) can mean to touch, strike, or come into contact with, depending on context.
But here is the crucial question.
Was God forbidding believers from respectfully examining a pastor's interpretation of Scripture?
No.
The psalm recalls God's protection of His people during the patriarchal period, when they were vulnerable among nations and rulers.
It is not a blanket prohibition against asking spiritual leaders questions.
And even when we consider David's refusal to harm Saul, the distinction remains important.
David would not kill Saul to seize the throne.
Yet David did not pretend Saul's conduct was righteous.
He confronted Saul's wrongdoing while refusing to take vengeance into his own hands.
Respect did not require pretending evil was good.
Restraint did not require denying the truth.
And honoring God's authority did not mean declaring every action of a human leader beyond examination.
We must be careful not to turn a passage about God's protection into a weapon that prevents accountability.
Because when Scripture is used to silence legitimate concerns, the problem is no longer merely poor leadership.
It becomes a distortion of the very Word that was given to protect and guide God's people.
And perhaps this is where the subject becomes painfully personal.
Some people are not afraid to ask questions because they lack courage.
They are afraid because they have already learned what happens when they do.
They have watched others become the subject of sermons after raising concerns.
They have seen friendships disappear.
They have been told that leaving a particular congregation means abandoning God's will.
They have heard that their family will suffer if they withdraw financial support.
They have been made to feel that disagreement with a pastor is equivalent to grieving the Holy Spirit.
And over time, something happens.
They stop asking.
Then they stop thinking aloud.
Then they stop trusting their own ability to read Scripture.
Eventually, they may begin confusing fear of a leader with reverence for God.
But Scripture never commands Christians to worship their shepherds.
It commands shepherds to care for the flock.
Listen to the apostle Peter.
In 1 Peter 5:2–3, he instructs elders to shepherd God's flock willingly and faithfully, concluding with these words:
“Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.”
The Greek expression κατακυριεύοντες (katakyrieuontes) describes exercising mastery or domineering over others.
Peter explicitly warns against that posture.
This is remarkable.
Peter himself was an apostle.
Yet he did not tell church elders to establish unquestionable personal control.
He told them not to domineer.
Instead, they were to become examples.
And a few verses earlier, he reminds them that the flock belongs to God.
Not to them.
A congregation is not a pastor's possession.
It is Christ's Church.
And the Chief Shepherd will appear.
That means every sermon, every counseling conversation, every disciplinary decision, every financial appeal, and every exercise of spiritual influence takes place beneath the gaze of Jesus.
Pastors are not merely managing an organization.
They are handling souls.
Souls Christ purchased with His own blood.
That reality should produce tenderness, not entitlement.
Humility, not intimidation.
A willingness to explain, not a demand to be unquestioned.
But we must also confront the other side of this issue.
Because not every question is innocent.
Not every disagreement is righteous.
And not everyone who says, “I'm just seeking truth,” is actually seeking truth.
Sometimes people question pastors because they are unwilling to receive correction.
Sometimes they want a leader who will affirm what Scripture condemns.
Sometimes they spread private suspicions publicly before seeking clarification.
Sometimes they interpret every difficult sermon as a personal attack.
Sometimes they demand perfection from a pastor while excusing bitterness in themselves.
And sometimes what begins as a legitimate concern becomes a campaign of humiliation, gossip, or revenge.
That is not biblical discernment.
That is sin wearing the language of accountability.
Scripture warns against it.
Numbers 16 records the rebellion of Korah and those who challenged Moses and Aaron.
Their rebellion was not simply that they asked a sincere question.
It involved a direct challenge to the leadership God had appointed, driven by a dispute over authority and position.
The account should make us cautious about prideful attempts to seize spiritual authority.
But it must not be stretched into a claim that every question directed toward a pastor is another Korah rebellion.
That would ignore both the actual context of Numbers 16 and the Bereans' example in Acts 17.
We need the whole counsel of God.
Not isolated verses selected to protect whichever side we already favor.
Proverbs 18:13 warns against answering a matter before hearing it.
Proverbs 18:17 reminds us that the first account of a dispute can appear convincing until another person examines it.
Those principles matter whether you are the pastor being accused or the church member raising a concern.
Truth deserves patience.
People deserve fairness.
And reputations should not be destroyed by rumors.
First Timothy 5:19 also provides an important safeguard regarding accusations against elders, requiring two or three witnesses before an accusation is received.
This is not a command to ignore credible reports of abuse, silence victims, or prevent appropriate investigation.
It is a warning against treating unsupported allegations as established guilt.

When abuse, exploitation, or criminal conduct is alleged, churches should take safety seriously, preserve evidence, involve appropriate independent authorities, and comply with applicable reporting laws.
A private meeting with an accused leader is not always safe or appropriate.
Biblical accountability must never become a system that protects the powerful at the expense of the vulnerable.
And genuine justice does not require abandoning fairness.
Both truths matter.
Now, imagine a different conversation.
A church member approaches a pastor after service.
“Pastor, may I ask you something? I was studying the passage you preached, and I struggled to understand how you reached that conclusion.”
The pastor could respond defensively.
“How dare you question me?”
Or he could say:
“Of course. Let's look at the passage together.”
Those responses reveal very different understandings of spiritual leadership.
The second response does not mean the pastor must agree with the member.
It means he recognizes that the Bible is not threatened by honest examination.
And perhaps, during that conversation, the member discovers they misunderstood the passage.
What a blessing.
They grow.
Or perhaps the pastor realizes he expressed something poorly.
What a blessing.
He grows.
Or perhaps they still disagree on a secondary theological issue, but they part with mutual respect and a shared commitment to Christ.
What a blessing.
Because Christian maturity is not demonstrated by never having difficult conversations.
It is demonstrated by learning to have them truthfully and lovingly.
Ephesians 4:15 calls believers to speak the truth in love.
Not truth without love.
Not love without truth.
Both.
And if your pastor corrects you from Scripture, receive that correction humbly.
You may discover that the problem was not his teaching but your interpretation.
Yet if a pastor refuses all examination, repeatedly manipulates Scripture, or uses spiritual threats to prevent legitimate accountability, do not assume your conscience must remain silent.
Seek wise, biblically grounded counsel.
Examine the evidence carefully.
And remember that faithfulness to Christ sometimes requires difficult decisions.
There is a striking example in Galatians 2.
Paul recounts confronting Peter at Antioch.
Peter had withdrawn from eating with Gentile believers under pressure from certain people.
His behavior compromised the truth expressed in the Gospel.
And Paul says in Galatians 2:11:
“I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.”
Think about that.
Peter.
The apostle who preached at Pentecost.
The man who had walked with Jesus.
The disciple who had witnessed the empty tomb.
He was corrected publicly by another apostle because his conduct was inconsistent with the Gospel.
The issue was serious and had public consequences, which helps explain the public correction.
This passage is not permission to publicly shame every pastor over every disagreement.
But it proves that prominent spiritual authority does not place someone beyond correction.
Peter's apostolic standing did not make his behavior automatically right.
And Paul's confrontation was not presented as rebellion against Christ.
It was a defense of Gospel truth.
That distinction matters more than many people realize.
The Church becomes spiritually dangerous when protecting a leader's image becomes more important than protecting the truth of the Gospel.
And yet there is something equally dangerous about a Christian who becomes so consumed with exposing flawed leaders that they stop loving the Church Christ died for.
Jesus did not shed His blood so that we could build our identities around suspicion.
He came to save sinners.
Including sinful pastors.
Including wounded church members.
Including proud critics.
Including fearful followers.
Including you.
Including me.
Every one of us stands in need of grace.
And this is where the entire conversation must move away from personalities and return to the cross.
Because the central question is not simply, “Can I question my pastor?”
The deeper question is, “Who ultimately owns my allegiance?”
When Jesus stood before religious authorities, He did not treat religious position as proof of righteousness.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He exposed those who placed burdens on others while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
In Matthew 23, His words are severe.
But His confrontation was not rooted in petty resentment.
It flowed from truth and from His holy concern for people being misled.
And in Matthew 20:25–28, Jesus taught His disciples that leadership in His kingdom must not imitate the domineering patterns of worldly rulers.
He said:
“Whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister.”
The word translated “minister” is διάκονος (diakonos), commonly associated with a servant or one who serves.
Jesus then pointed to Himself.
“The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.”
There is the model.
Not a throne built upon people's fear.
A Savior kneeling in service.
Not authority used to extract unquestioning loyalty.
Authority expressed through sacrificial love.
Not a shepherd demanding that sheep protect his reputation at all costs.
The Good Shepherd laying down His life for the sheep.
Jesus did not merely teach servant leadership.
He embodied it.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed the despised.
He washed His disciples' feet.
He endured betrayal.
He carried a cross.
And when sinful humanity displayed its ugliest violence against Him, He accomplished redemption through His death and resurrection.
That is the Gospel.
The sinless Son of God died for sinners, was buried, and rose again.
Our hope is not that we can find a flawless pastor.
Our hope is that we have a flawless Savior.
Our salvation does not rest upon the reputation of a ministry.
It rests upon the finished work of Jesus Christ.
And when we repent and trust in Him, we are not merely recruited into a religious institution.
We are reconciled to God.
Forgiven.
Adopted.
Given new life.
Called to walk in truth.
This is why spiritual authority must always remain accountable to Scripture.
Because the moment we make a human leader functionally untouchable, we risk giving that leader a place that belongs to Christ alone.
And the moment we reject all spiritual authority because some leaders have failed us, we risk refusing a gift God intended for our growth.
The answer is neither blind obedience nor permanent distrust.
The answer is Christ-centered discernment.
Honor your pastor.
Pray for him.
Encourage him.
Remember that he may be carrying burdens you cannot see.
He may be counseling marriages that are collapsing.
He may be praying over a dying church member.
He may be trying to provide for his family while carrying the expectations of an entire congregation.
He may be exhausted.
He may be lonely.
He may have made mistakes he deeply regrets.
Do not treat him as disposable simply because he is imperfect.
But do not treat him as divine because he is gifted.
A powerful sermon does not make a person incapable of error.
A large congregation does not guarantee sound doctrine.
Miraculous claims do not remove the need for biblical testing.
A respected title does not erase the need for integrity.
And years of faithful ministry do not grant immunity from accountability.
First Thessalonians 5:21 says:
“Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.”
In context, Paul is addressing the congregation's response to prophetic activity and the need for discernment.
The Greek verb δοκιμάζετε (dokimazete) means to test, examine, or assess something to determine its genuineness.
The principle is clear.
Christians should not be gullible.
Nor should they be cynical.
We are to test carefully and hold on to what is good.
That includes our own motives.
Before challenging a pastor, ask yourself whether you have understood his teaching fairly.
Have you studied the passage in context?
Are you seeking clarification or merely trying to win?
Are you willing to be corrected?
Are you motivated by love for Christ and His people?
Have you distinguished a biblical command from a personal preference?
And before dismissing a member's question, pastors should ask themselves equally searching questions.
Have I explained the Scripture faithfully?
Am I confusing my authority with God's authority?
Am I responding to a sincere concern as though it were a personal attack?
Am I willing to acknowledge an error?
Have I created an environment where people can tell the truth without fearing retaliation?
Do I care more about shepherding this person than protecting my image?
These are uncomfortable questions.
But sometimes uncomfortable questions become instruments of grace.
Sometimes repentance begins when we finally stop defending ourselves long enough to hear what God is exposing.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking possibility is this.
Somewhere today, a believer is considering walking away from Jesus because someone claiming to represent Jesus wounded them.
They were not simply disappointed by a sermon.
They were spiritually crushed.
They were told that their questions made them unfaithful.
Their sincere concerns were dismissed.
Their trust was broken.
And now, every time they hear the word “church,” their stomach tightens.
Every time someone says “submit,” they remember being controlled.
Every time a pastor speaks about honor, they hear the voice of someone who demanded loyalty but refused accountability.
If that describes you, please hear this.
What happened in a church does not determine who Jesus is.
A leader's failure does not invalidate Christ's faithfulness.
A distorted interpretation of Scripture does not make Scripture itself untrustworthy.
And the sins of people who carry God's name do not erase the holiness of the God whose name they carry.
You do not have to call evil good in order to forgive.
You do not have to return to an unsafe environment to prove that you trust Jesus.
You do not have to deny what happened to demonstrate grace.
Forgiveness, reconciliation, restored trust, and restored leadership are related but distinct matters.
Repentance matters.
Accountability matters.
Safety matters.
And genuine restoration cannot be manufactured by demanding that wounded people pretend nothing happened.
But please do not let a false picture of Jesus steal your desire to know the real Jesus.
Open the Gospels again.
Watch how He treats the broken.
Watch how He responds to sincere seekers.
Watch Him confront hypocrisy.
Watch Him welcome repentant sinners.
Watch Him restore Peter after Peter's devastating denial.
Watch Him call people out of darkness without exploiting their shame.
There is no Savior like Him.
And there is something else you need to remember.
The same Peter whom Paul later confronted was the Peter whom Jesus had already restored.
Failure did not have to be the end of Peter's story.
And correction did not have to mean rejection.
In John 21, the risen Jesus asked Peter whether he loved Him.
Then He entrusted Peter with the care of His sheep.
“Feed my sheep.”
Not “Own my sheep.”
Not “Control my sheep.”
Not “Make my sheep afraid to question you.”
Feed them.
Love them.
Care for them.
That is the heartbeat of Christian shepherding.
And it is why pastors themselves need the Gospel every day.
They need grace when they fail.
They need courage when they must confront sin.
They need humility when corrected.
They need wisdom when criticized unfairly.
They need brothers and sisters who will pray for them rather than flatter them.
And they need to remember that they are sheep before they are shepherds.
They belong to Jesus too.
Maybe you are reading this as a pastor.
And perhaps something in these words has unsettled you.
Maybe you remember a member you dismissed too quickly.
Maybe you used your position to win an argument when you should have opened your Bible.
Maybe you have been so wounded by criticism that you now interpret every question as an attack.
There is grace for repentance.
You can apologize.
You can correct a teaching.
You can invite accountability.
You can seek help.
You can become a safer, wiser, more Christlike shepherd.
Not by pretending you have never failed.
But by refusing to let pride keep you from the transforming work of Jesus.
Or maybe you are reading this as someone who has spent years criticizing pastors.
You know every controversy.
You can identify every doctrinal weakness.
You have become skilled at exposing what is wrong.
But somewhere along the way, compassion disappeared.
You no longer pray for the people you criticize.
You no longer grieve over sin.
You enjoy the downfall of leaders you dislike.
If that is true, you also need to return to the cross.
Because discernment without love can become cruelty.
And truth used as a weapon of personal vengeance does not reflect the heart of Christ.
The Gospel calls us to something deeper than being right in an argument.
It calls us to become like Jesus.
And perhaps you are the quiet believer who started reading this article with tears already close to the surface.
You have been wondering whether God is angry with you for asking questions.
You have been replaying conversations in your head.
You have been frightened that your doubts mean you are losing your faith.
You have even wondered whether your desire to understand Scripture is evidence that your heart is rebellious.
Please understand the distinction.
A question asked in humility is not automatically rebellion.
A concern raised in love is not automatically dishonor.
A request for biblical explanation is not automatically an attack on authority.
And refusing a command that contradicts God's Word is not disobedience to God.
But your questions must still be brought before Him.
Let Scripture examine your motives as carefully as you examine another person's teaching.
Be willing to repent if you have acted pridefully.
Be willing to forgive where forgiveness is needed.
Be willing to receive correction.
Be willing to pursue peace where peace is possible.
And be willing to stand for truth when standing becomes costly.
Because following Jesus has never meant avoiding every difficult conversation.
Sometimes faithfulness sounds like a respectful question.
Sometimes it sounds like an apology.
Sometimes it sounds like a courageous correction.
Sometimes it sounds like refusing to participate in wrongdoing.
And sometimes it sounds like a wounded believer whispering a prayer they have not had the strength to pray in months.
“Lord Jesus, I still want to trust You. Please help me see You clearly again.”
That prayer matters.
Not because the words are impressive.
But because Christ is merciful.
He does not despise the brokenhearted who come to Him.
And He does not require you to understand every mystery before you can cling to His grace.
So should Christians question their pastors?
Yes, when there is a genuine need to seek understanding, test teaching against Scripture, or address legitimate concerns.
But they should do so with humility, fairness, love, and a willingness to be corrected themselves.
Should Christians honor and submit to faithful pastoral leadership?
Yes.
Scripture teaches that too.
And can questioning a pastor become rebellion?
Certainly.
When it grows from pride, contempt, dishonest accusation, divisiveness, or refusal to heed sound biblical correction, it can become sinful.
But asking a question is not itself the sin.
The heart, the truth of the concern, the manner of the approach, and the response to God's Word all matter.
The Church does not need fewer people who think carefully about Scripture.
It needs more people who love Scripture enough to obey it.
It does not need pastors who are terrified of accountability.
It needs shepherds who welcome the refining work of truth.
It does not need congregations that celebrate rebellion.
It needs disciples who understand the difference between godly submission and blind loyalty.
And above everything, it needs Jesus Christ at the center.
Not celebrity.
Not personality.
Not institutional pride.
Not religious intimidation.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The Chief Shepherd.
The One whose authority is perfect because His character is perfect.
The One who never manipulates His sheep to preserve a fragile ego.
The One who speaks truth because He is truth.
The One who corrects those He loves.
The One who welcomes sinners who repent.
The One who can redeem even the most painful chapters of our spiritual history.
From fear to truth.
From manipulation to freedom in Christ.
From wounded faith to renewed trust in the Savior who has never failed.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not to win an argument.
Not to expose your pastor.
Not to encourage public accusations.
But because someone reading your words may be silently carrying the same struggle.
Have you ever been afraid to ask a sincere biblical question because you thought it would be called rebellion?
Or have you been a pastor who was deeply hurt by questions asked without love?
You might simply comment, “Lord, teach me to honor without blindly following.”
Or, if your faith has been wounded, “Jesus, help me trust You again.”
And if you are a pastor seeking to lead more faithfully, perhaps your prayer is, “Lord, make me a shepherd after Your heart.”
Your honesty may encourage someone who thought they were the only one.
Return to the Scriptures. Study them in context. Let God's Word continue the conversation long after you have finished reading.
If you have been strengthened by this message, I also want to invite you into something deeper.
Our desire is to build a community that continues growing in Scripture, repentance, healing, discipleship, and the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our commitment to make biblical encouragement and discipleship more accessible.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Not because you must pay to prove your faith.
Not because grace, biblical truth, or spiritual growth can be purchased.
But because voluntary generosity can help a ministry continue serving people.
If you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel-centered teaching, this is one meaningful opportunity to do so.
Because the ultimate goal is not to build a platform around a human personality.
It is to point people to the One whose name is above every name.
Jesus Christ.
And maybe the greatest thing you take away from this article is not a new argument about church authority.
Maybe it is the courage to open your Bible again.
To ask a sincere question without hatred.
To honor a faithful pastor without idolizing him.
To receive correction without humiliation.
To forgive without pretending wrongdoing was harmless.
To stand for truth without losing love.
To return to Christian fellowship with wisdom rather than fear.
And to remember that your relationship with God was never meant to depend upon another human being's perfection.
Because on the day you stand before Christ, the question will not be whether you protected every decision your pastor ever made.
The question will be whether you belonged to Jesus, trusted His grace, and followed Him faithfully.
So hold your Bible close.
Keep your heart humble.
Love the Church.
Pray for your shepherds.
Test what you hear.
Repent when you are wrong.
Speak when truth requires courage.
And never forget whose sheep you are.
The voice that was meant to lead you to Jesus must never become the voice that keeps you afraid to follow Him.
